heading: Ninety-three parishes
lead: David asked us to work through the people one by one until they are done. This is what that produced first — not a list of people, but **the map they were standing on**. Nine hundred and fifty-four indexed records of this surname in Croatia, every one traced from index entry to image, from image to film, and from film to the parish register it was filmed from. **Ninety-three parishes.** This archive had eighteen.

why.text:
The Croatian index usually gives no parish. It says «**Croazia, Austria**», or «Hrvatska», or nothing — which is why a year of searching produced towns only where a transcriber had happened to type one. But **every persona carries the ark of the image it was read from**, the digital-archive service turns that ark into a **DGS film number**, and the catalogue names the film's parish. Do that for every record and the map draws itself.

Nine hundred and fifty-four records, **196 distinct films**, ninety-three parishes. It is mechanical, it is repeatable, and it took an afternoon.

The four biggest concentrations are the four this archive already follows, in almost the order it would have guessed: **Omiš 145** records from 1634, **Rijeka 105** from 1626, **Ližnjan 100**, **Svetvinčenat 85** from 1666, **Pula 63** from 1659. And **Bakar gives exactly five, 1772–1819** — which is the household this archive reconstructed and dated, to the year, from a different direction.

**Ližnjan's hundred records begin in 1794.** Not 1667, not 1700 — 1794. The southern-Istrian line's own parish is a *late* register, and the early southern entries this archive has leaned on are Pula's (from **1659**) and Svetvinčenat's (from **1666**). Pula's run is real and it is the oldest in the south; the specific 1667 and 1669 baptisms this archive called «Pula» are Svetvinčenat's. Both things are true and the page now says both.

Six places this archive has never named, and one of them is large.

**Vižinada — 53 records, 1790–1860.** Bigger than Kaštelir and Poreč together, in western Istria between Motovun and the coast, and completely absent from this site until today. **Draguč — 25, 1784–1851**, in the Buzet country. **Rovinj — 23, from 1619**, the earliest date in the entire map. **Dubrovnik — 38** across the city parish and Pile, 1741–1862, plus Orašac and the hospital: a Ragusan presence nobody here suspected. **Bednja 13 from 1706 and Pregrada 7 from 1674** — the Hrvatsko zagorje, three hundred kilometres inland and older than most of Istria. And a long tail through continental Croatia and the islands: Đurđevac, Đakovo, Karlovac, Križevci, Orahovica, Lepoglava, Samobor, Petrinja, Vukovar, Nerežišća on Brač, Cres, Rab, Pag, Olib, Hvar, Korčula, Murter, Skradin.

**It does not join anybody to anybody.** A parish map is a map of a surname, not of a family, and this one now has ninety-three points on it precisely because the name is common. What it does is tell this archive **which registers to open**, in what order, and stop it guessing at place-names the index never gave. Vižinada is the first of the new ones, because fifty-three records in seventy years is a household and not a scatter.

source_pm: FamilySearch record index, collection 2040054 «Croatia, church books, 1516–1994», swept for the surname in every spelling and every date window reachable, September 2026: 954 personas, each resolved to its image ark, each ark resolved through the digital-archive service to a DGS film number, and each film identified in the FamilySearch catalogue. Counts are of indexed records, not of people — one person may be indexed twice, and an unindexed register contributes nothing.
